sections.label: Bill on abuse of process
sections.summary: The Bill aims to safeguard the administration of justice by clarifying that egregious abuse of court process amounts to contempt of court.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: This Bill is intended to safeguard the administration of justice in Singapore by clarifying that egregious abuse of the court process will amount to contempt of court.

sections.label: Administration of Justice (Protection) Act 2016
sections.summary: In 2016, the House passed the Administration of Justice (Protection) Act, known as AOJPA.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: In 2016, this House passed the Administration of Justice (Protection) Act, or AOJPA in short.

sections.label: Examples of egregious abuse of process
sections.summary: Contempt by interference with justice may be committed by egregiously abusing court process, with examples including baseless claims, fictitious claims to delay proceedings, and meritless actions.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Contempt by interference with the administration of justice may be committed in various ways, including by abusing the process of the court in an egregious manner.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Examples of such egregious abuse include: (a) commencing civil proceedings to seek financial damages, despite knowing that the claim is without foundation, for the ulterior motive of oppressing the defendant; (b) filing fictitious claims for the improper purpose of delaying criminal proceedings; and (c) persistently commencing actions and making applications that are totally without merit.

sections.label: Clarificatory amendments to contempt threshold
sections.summary: The proposed amendments are clarificatory, do not lower the contempt threshold, and make clear that egregious abuse of process can attract criminal sanctions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: The amendments which we are proposing are, therefore, clarificatory in nature.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: They do not lower the current threshold for contempt of Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: The amendments will make it clear to the public and potential court users that egregious cases of abuse of process will amount to contempt of court and that such conduct can attract criminal sanctions.

sections.label: Application to all court proceedings
sections.summary: The new provisions apply to all court proceedings in Singapore, whether conducted by a self-represented person or a lawyer.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: The new provisions apply to all court proceedings in Singapore, whether conducted by a self-represented person or a lawyer.

sections.label: Liability for causing or abetting abuse
sections.summary: Clause 2(d) provides that persons who cause or abet egregious abuse of court process under new section 3(1)(da) and (db) will also be liable for contempt.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: To deter such behaviour, clause 2(d) of the Bill provides that persons who cause or abet egregious abuse of our court process as provided for under the new section 3(1)(da) and (db) will also be liable for contempt.

sections.label: Narrower contempt categories than Chee Siok Chin
sections.summary: The Bill's provisions specify narrower categories of contempt than those set out in Chee Siok Chin, to capture only egregious cases.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: To ensure that we only capture egregious cases as contempt, the provisions in the Bill specify narrower categories than what was set out in Chee Siok Chin.

sections.label: Amendments clarificatory, threshold unchanged
sections.summary: The amendments are clarificatory and do not lower the current threshold for contempt of court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: First, I reiterate that the amendments are clarificatory in nature and do not lower the current threshold for contempt of court.

sections.label: Standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt
sections.summary: The standard of proof remains proof beyond a reasonable doubt under section 28 of the AOJPA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: The standard of proof remains that of proof beyond a reasonable doubt under section 28 of the AOJPA.

sections.label: Lawyers' practical challenges and reasonable steps
sections.summary: The standard allows the Court to consider lawyers' practical challenges, but a lawyer who fails to take reasonable steps may be caught by the amendments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: The standard also allows the Court to take into account the practical challenges faced by the lawyers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: However, in the same scenario, if the lawyer had failed to take reasonable steps – for example, by ignoring obvious red flags, or had carried on conducting the application even after discovering that the new evidence was fabricated – then, he may well be caught by the amendments.

sections.label: Deterring abuse of court process
sections.summary: The amendments clarify that severe abuse of court process, such as knowingly deceitful, sham or baseless proceedings, will be treated as contempt of court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: The proposed amendments will help us deter egregious cases of abuse of process and safeguard our justice system so that it continues to benefit and serve all of us.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: As I have elaborated in some detail in going through the amendments, they are clarificatory and are not intended to lower the threshold for contempt.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: So, while hon Members may have brought prepared speeches, I would ask that you may want to consider the explanations I have already given, so that the response I may provide later can be more efficient.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: These amendments clarify that severe cases of abuse of court process, where proceedings are knowingly initiated with deceit, as shams or based on baseless claims, these will be treated as contempt of court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: I welcome the hon Minister of State's assurance that this Bill does not lower the threshold for contempt, but it is meant to deter abuse of our Courts, and thus preserving the Courts' integrity for those with genuine claims.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: These amendments are welcome in light of the observations from the High Court in the recent case that the Minister of State mentioned, where an applicant filed for judicial review with the ulterior aim of delaying his punishment of caning.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: This Bill addresses situations where litigants or their advocates knowingly file abusive applications.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: It reinforces that the Court is a place for genuine grievances, not tactical delays or gamesmanship.

sections.label: Farid Batra re-sentenced to life imprisonment
sections.summary: Farid Batra was initially sentenced to death for drug trafficking but was later re-sentenced to life imprisonment and 15 strokes of the cane.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In Farid Batra's case, he was initially sentenced to death for drug trafficking but was later certified by the Prosecution to be a courier who had rendered substantive assistance, which led to the Court re-sentencing him to life imprisonment and 15 strokes of the cane.

sections.label: New contempt of court provisions
sections.summary: Clause 2 introduces section 3(da) and proposed section 3D(b) making certain court proceedings contempt of court.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Clause 2 of the Bill introduces a new section 3(da), which will make it a contempt of court for any person to conduct or commence a court proceeding when he knows or ought to know that the proceeding involves a deception of the court, is fictitious or constitutes a mere sham.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Bill also introduced a proposed section 3D(b), where it will also amount to contempt if a person conducts or commences multiple or successive court proceedings when he knows all to know that such proceedings are manifestly groundless and without foundation.

sections.label: High Court contempt penalties
sections.summary: A contempt of the High Court carries a potential fine of up to $100,000 and up to three years' jail.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: For example, a contempt of the High Court carries a potential fine of up to $100,000 and a jail term of up to three years.

sections.label: Farid Batra judge's observation
sections.summary: In Farid Batra's case the Judge said a lawyer could expect substantial severe consequences, suggesting sufficient measures against lawyers.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In the case of Farid Batra, who had no lawyer representing him in the latest case, the Judge observed that if he were represented by a lawyer and I quote the Judge here, "The lawyer could expect substantial severe consequences." This appears to be an acknowledgement by the Court that there are already sufficient disciplinary and deterrent measures against lawyers.

sections.label: Consultation on the Bill
sections.summary: MinLaw said stakeholders including the Judiciary were consulted, and the speaker asks whether the Law Society was consulted and its views.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: MinLaw has stated in its October press release that key stakeholders had been consulted on the Bill, including the Judiciary.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Earlier, the Minister of State mentioned that he spoke to several members of the Bar as well.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: But I would like to ask whether the Law Society was specifically consulted and, if so, what were its views?

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Could the Ministry further clarify why the existing framework for disciplining lawyers is not adequate to handle the scenarios emphasised by the Bill?

sections.label: Safeguards for genuine claims
sections.summary: The speaker seeks clarification on how amendments differentiate genuine claims from contemptuous ones and what safeguards protect individuals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Yet, we must be cautious that the tightening of contempt provisions does not stifle legitimate discourse.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Thus, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I seek clarification on how the amendments will differentiate between genuine claims, if even unsuccessful, and those deemed contemptuous.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: What safeguards are in place to protect individuals who may unintentionally bring forward claims, later classified as groundless?

sections.label: Public education campaigns
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether public education campaigns are planned to help residents understand what constitutes a manifestly groundless claim.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Are there plans to conduct public education campaigns to help residents understand what constitutes a manifestly groundless claim?

sections.label: Guidelines for legal advisors
sections.summary: Asks whether clearer guidelines on "ought to have known" are needed and whether heightened liability could raise legal costs for residents.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Should there be clearer guidelines for legal advisors on what constitutes "ought to have known" when assessing case merit, could heightened liability raise legal costs for residents as lawyers factor in greater risk?

sections.label: Fair and balanced justice system
sections.summary: Calls for a fair, balanced system that deters abuse without discouraging genuine claims, and states the Bill clarifies egregious abuses of court process are contempt.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: As we implement these changes, let us make sure that they achieve a fair and balanced system, one that deters abuse without discouraging genuine claims, supports vulnerable residents, respects the role of our legal advisors and strengthens public trust in our Judiciary.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: This is a call for a justice system that is not just efficient, but compassionate and accessible to all Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: I urge the Ministry to provide the necessary clarifications and safeguards so that this Bill can truly protect the integrity of our courts while honouring the rights of our residents.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Let us, together, build a justice system that inspires confidence and upholds the principles we all stand by.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: This Bill clarifies that egregious abuses of court process amounts to contempt of court.

sections.label: Contempt for sham proceedings
sections.summary: New section 3(1)(da) makes it contempt of court to conduct or commence proceedings involving deception, being fictitious or a mere sham.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The new section 3(1)(da) makes it contempt of court to conduct or commence proceedings if they involve a deception of the court, are fictitious or constitutes a mere sham.

sections.label: Liability for causing sham filings
sections.summary: Under new section 3(7), individuals who cause or abet parties or advocates to file sham or groundless proceedings may be accountable for contempt.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Under the new section 3(7), individuals who cause or abet parties or advocates to file sham or groundless proceedings may be accountable for contempt of court.

sections.label: Support for litigants
sections.summary: States that non-government organisation support is important for some litigants, which is why the State Courts have the Friend Scheme.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: For some litigants, support from non-government organisations is very important in helping them in navigating the legal system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: This is the reason why the State Courts have its Community Courts and Tribunals Clusters Friend Scheme.

sections.label: Clarificatory amendments
sections.summary: States that the amendments in the Bill reflect current law and are clarificatory in nature.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: The amendments in the Bill reflect what is already the current law and are clarificatory in nature.

sections.label: Contempt threshold unchanged
sections.summary: The amendments do not lower the current threshold for contempt of court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: The amendments do not lower the current threshold for contempt of court.

sections.label: Genuine claims unaffected
sections.summary: The amendments in the Bill will not affect genuine claims.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: The amendments we are introducing in the Bill will not affect such genuine claims.

sections.label: Meritless case not contempt
sections.summary: A case found to be without merit is insufficient by itself to amount to contempt of court under the amendments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: On the phrase "manifestly groundless or without foundation", an important point for hon Members to note is that even if the case is found to be without merit, that, in itself, is insufficient to amount to contempt of court under the amendments.

sections.label: Non-parties caught under section 3(7)
sections.summary: Non-parties are caught under new section 3(7) only if the Court finds they caused or abetted abuse of process and knew or ought to have known of its abusive nature.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: Under the Bill, non-parties will only be caught under the new section 3(7) if the Court finds that the non-party: one, caused or abetted the types of abuse of process set out in sections 3(1)(da) and 3(1)(db); and two, knew or ought to have known of the abusive nature of the court proceeding.

sections.label: Lawyers and egregious abuse
sections.summary: Lawyers acting with reasonable care and good faith have nothing to fear, and the amendments only capture egregious abuse of process.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: As I elaborated in some detail in my opening speech, lawyers who act with reasonable care and in good faith have nothing to fear.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: I should also stress that the amendments only capture egregious abuse of process.

sections.label: Existing levers for less serious cases
sections.summary: Existing levers such as cost orders may be appropriate for less serious cases but may not be adequate for egregious abuse of process.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: The existing levers, such as cost orders, may be appropriate for less serious cases, but may not be adequate for egregious cases of abuse of process.

sections.label: Mental element of abusive applications
sections.summary: The provisions require a person to have known or ought to have known of the abusive nature of the application, assessed by a contextual reasonableness standard.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: The mental element provided for in the provisions is that the person must have known or ought to have known of the abusive nature of the application.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: On the standard on "ought to have known", the question for the court to assess, is whether the person could have reasonably known of the abusive nature of the application.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: This is a contextual standard of reasonableness, which would not capture those who act with reasonable care and good faith.

sections.label: Public reporting of contempt cases
sections.summary: Mr Yip Hon Weng suggested more detailed public reporting, and the speaker said more may be considered but contempt cases are already publicly reported.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: Mr Yip Hon Weng likewise suggested more detailed public reporting.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: We will consider if more can be done to raise public awareness in this area.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: However, I should add that cases involving contempt of court are already publicly reported when the Court issues its judgment.

sections.label: Senior lawyers on safeguarding justice
sections.summary: Senior members of the Bar with extensive litigation experience reached consensus on the importance of safeguarding the justice system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: These were senior members of the Bar across various practice groups with extensive experience in litigation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: There was consensus on the importance of safeguarding our justice system.
